1 In regione Chorassan, quam Graeco nomine Theophilus Margianam nuncupat,
temporibus chalifarum Al-Mansur et Al-Mahdi perpetuo seditiones exortae sunt
quae duces eorum armis compresserunt (cf. Weil, Gesch. der Chalifen, t. II, 1848,
pp. 36, 66, 161). Sed utique ante annum 768, quo Theophilus scripsisse videtur
(supra p. 232 a), haec expeditio, cui alludit, suscepta est. Agitur sine dubio de
tumultu quem praeses huius provinciae Chazim ibn Chuzeima novarum rerum cupi-
dus annis 757-758 movit. Nam exercitui qui eum debellavit, interfuisse principem
regium Al Mahdi, postea (775) chalifam, comperimus (Weil, op. cit., p. 36). Qui, si
haec recte coniecimus, iam cum iuvenis esset, Theophilum familiarem habebat. —
Ceterum Abassidae in bellis astrologos secum duxisse solebant, nam et mathe-
maticus Persa Jahjâ ben Abî Mansûr Tarsi obiit, cum Chalifam Al-Mamum adver-
sus Graecos pugnantem comitaretur (Suter, Astronomen der Araber, p. 8, n° 14).
sections.en: 1 In the region of Khorasan, which Theophilus calls by the Greek name Margiana, in the times of the caliphs Al-Mansur and Al-Mahdi, seditions continually arose which their generals suppressed by arms (cf. Weil, Gesch. der Chalifen, vol. II, 1848, pp. 36, 66, 161). But certainly before the year 768, in which Theophilus seems to have written (above p. 232 a), this expedition, to which he alludes, was undertaken. It is undoubtedly about the tumult which the governor of this province, Khazim ibn Khuzayma, desirous of revolution, set in motion in the years 757-758. For we find that the royal prince Al-Mahdi, later (775) caliph, was present in the army which defeated him (Weil, op. cit., p. 36). He, if we have conjectured these things correctly, already when he was a young man, had Theophilus as an intimate. — Moreover, the Abbasids were accustomed to take astrologers with them in wars, for also the Persian mathematician Yahya ibn Abi Mansur died at Tarsus, when he was accompanying the Caliph Al-Mamun fighting against the Greeks (Suter, Astronomen der Araber, p. 8, no. 14).

summary.headline: Theophilus on Military Astrology
summary.text: Theophilus explains that he derived reliable military inceptions from genethlialogical and catarchic astrology during an expedition to Margiana, covering warfare, tyrannies, and besieged cities. He instructs readers to blend zodiacal signs, wandering and fixed stars, luminaries, lots, and their lords; a second-edition preface then opens with his letter to his son Deucalion defending mathematical science through scriptural and philosophical testimony.
